title: Journalists in Africa and South America Are Mapping the Mines Devouring the World’s Rainforests
content:
In the Amazon and Congo rainforests, investigative journalists are using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence (AI) to expose groups that operate in secret, extracting gold and minerals from some of the world’s most remote regions.

In the Amazon, journalists have mapped thousands of sites where armed groups are clearing forests to mine gold. In the Congo, journalists are identifying areas where artisanal miners use buckets and shovels to illegally extract cobalt and copper.

The projects are on separate continents but face similar challenges: limited resources, dangerous terrain and powerful interests that want to keep their activities hidden. Now, journalists working with the Amazon Mining Watch and Africa Mining Watch projects are sharing strategies to automate parts of their investigations and build cross-border networks to strengthen their reporting.

title: Russian War Recruitment in Africa, Hidden West Bank Settlement Funding, Scams in Southeast Asia, and More: 2026 DIG Awards Shortlist
content:
From September 23 – 27, 2026, the 12th edition of the DIG Festival — Europe’s premier multimedia investigative journalism festival — will showcase a powerhouse lineup of outstanding investigative documentaries and podcasts for attendees in Modena, Italy.

These include the screening of 25 new investigative films — chosen from 300 entries — which will be evaluated by an international jury across five video categories for the annual DIG Awards. The diverse finalists reflect the theme of the 2026 event, “Bella Ciao,” which has emerged as a call to arms for free speech and democracy and recalls a World War II-era protest anthem.

The DIG jury, chaired this year by award-winning Croatian filmmaker Igor Bezinović, will also select winners from among five shortlisted investigative podcasts that tackle harms including systematic exploitation, corruption, and abuse.

title: ‘Once Someone Opens the Door and I Manage to Sit Down with them, I Have a Shot’: Colombia’s Ricardo Calderón on His Career Conducting High-Risk Investigations
content: The poster depicting a fountain pen emerging from the barrel of a revolver hung for many years behind Ricardo Calderón’s desk. It was an old cover from Le Nouvel Observateur, and the text above the image read: “Le pouvoir des journalistes,” the power of journalists. A colleague had bought it from a Paris flea market and brought it to the newsroom of Semana magazine in Bogotá, where Calderón worked for more than two decades as an investigative reporter. He loved the poster so much that he made a copy of it so he could see it every morning when he walked into his office.

title: Getting Started with Open Source Tools and Tips
content:
In this masterclass video, Sayyara Mammadova, associate director for capacity building at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab), shares her approach to open source investigations.

From cultivating curiosity and deconstructing other investigators’ work to tracing online entities back to real people, Mammadova explains why open source reporting is never about using a single tool or source, but a combination of methods that reinforce and verify each other. The video will help you understand why ethics and operational security are non-negotiable when handling open source data, why continuous training keeps investigators sharp as tools evolve, and why an adaptive mindset matters more than any single tool, because tools change but the ability to find information doesn’t have to.

title: Investigating Threats to Democracy and the Rise in Authoritarianism: IJ WEEK Sessions Focus
content:
Independent journalism continues to serve as one of the last lines of defense for democratic principles like public transparency, accountability, and human rights, as the world commemorates the International Day of Democracy — and reflects on the threats posed by rising authoritarianism.

In recognition of the need for new techniques and collaborations to counter these threats, the Global Investigative Journalism Network has tailored several major panels around the topic of democracy and the growing threat of authoritarianism at its upcoming IJ WEEK online event, which will be held online from October 26 – 30.

In addition, many of the nearly 50 sessions and online workshops — featuring more than 130 expert speakers — will showcase investigative techniques on topics closely bound up with the health of democracies, from climate change to corruption and Big Tech. The program will also include three separate sessions with winners of the 2026 Sigma Awards, where innovative methods for obtaining and analyzing public data and records will be shared, with deep relevance to reporting on governance everywhere.

title: German Far Right’s TikTok Reach, Iran War’s Impact on Cooking Gas, Mapping the Nepal Floods, and ‘Strongest’ Country Passports
content:
An election result in the German region of Saxony-Anhalt has highlighted the far right’s growing reach on social media, with Die Zeit examining how the party’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, dominated TikTok during the recent campaign. Our roundup of the Top 10 in Data Journalism, looking at stories from August 26 to September 8, also includes a New York Times 3D reconstruction of the deadly glacier collapse in Nepal, which killed more than 1,000 people. Elsewhere, we look at Bloomberg’s mapping of how LPG supply routes to India have been disrupted during the Iran war, Balady Atlas’ exploration of how the pilgrimages of Hajj and Umrah have changed, and La Nación’s analysis of the insults Argentine President Javier Milei has made in speeches and on social media.

title: ‘Praise Colleagues, Delegate, and Know That Mistakes are Inevitable’: Tips for Managers in Investigative Journalism
content:
Let’s be clear: Managing teams is not easy. You can master what you do, but guiding people is quite a different thing and it requires another set of skills.

I have been lucky enough to work under some great leaders. Some of them were journalists, others came from a different space, such as the civic tech field. They all taught me how to lead others strategically, but most importantly with kindness and respect. None of them were born managers or leaders, but all of them learned how to do it.

I’ve been thinking a lot about leadership recently — as something to grapple with alongside the day-to-day of producing our journalism at The Examination, where I’m in charge of the data team.

Some people might think that being a manager in the investigative journalism field should not be different from being a manager in other spaces. However, there are some specific aspects that make the role unique: working under pressure and thinking about people’s security and mental health all while working on complex stories.
snippet: Let’s be clear: Managing teams is not easy. You can master what you do, but guiding people is quite a different thing and it requires another set of skills.

title: Using Geospatial Data for Investigations
content:
How do you investigate places you can’t reach? In this masterclass video, Kuek Ser Kuang Keng, data editor at the Pulitzer Center, shows how (geo)spatial data can unlock stories in inaccessible or restricted areas.

From defining your hypothesis to sourcing and verifying data, he walks through the full workflow: where to find spatial data, how to handle its specific formats, and which tools to use, including QGIS, Google Earth, and Google My Maps.

The session focuses on practical uses: analyzing satellite imagery, comparing datasets over time, and presenting findings through maps and visuals that make complex investigations clear and compelling.

title: Guide to Investigating Tech and AI in Modern Warfare
content:
When historians look back on the wars of the 2020s, they may be struck by two things.

The first is that vast wells of content that traditionally helped such historians report on wars are completely missing. The modern equivalent of the diaries of the Great War? WhatsApp messages long deleted. The comparable typed-up Situation Reports — if they survived being destroyed — once found in the Vietnam War? Vanished on corroded servers. Immense tracts of digital data might be lost to time.

The second insight might be a struggle to locate the frontline of the fighting. Was it where civilians were most harmed? Was it the headquarters of a drone squadron? Was it on the servers of some tech giant? The physical geography of modern armed conflict, once defined by that thin red line of battle, has extended and extended, so that the operational frontline is harder and harder to place. A complex map of the digital battlefield would emerge, that would include satellite constellations, cloud contracts, server archives, and arms and tech supply chains.

title: ‘Denies Her the Justice She Deserves’: A Shocking Verdict in the Trial Over Daphne Caruana Galizia’s Murder
content:
Malta’s Courts of Justice are located at the heart of its capital, Valletta. Facing the neoclassical building stands a national monument turned makeshift memorial for journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

Photographs are placed on the stone of the memorial and in the soil around it, among placards and bouquets of flowers — some fresh, some a bit older. This protest memorial has been persistently maintained by activists for almost nine years, since Daphne’s assassination in October 2017. The memorial, frequently revived, acts as a manifestation of the consistent call for justice. Over the past two months, new candles were placed on the memorial and lit — some lighting up the word justice as dusk set in.

The protest memorial for Daphne Caruana Galizia at Malta’s Court of Justice, as seen during the trial. Image: Joanna Demarco for GIJN

The memorial could be seen through the window just outside of Hall 22, Malta’s biggest courtroom.

Inside, across from my seat on a bench in the press area of this courtroom hung a crucifix and a large Maltese coat of arms, its scroll slightly tilted.

title: Turning Copernicus Satellite Data Into Public-Interest Climate Stories
content:
Climate change is often reported through global records and international headlines. Yet its effects are experienced locally. Farmers adapt to changing seasons, coastal communities face warmer seas, and cities struggle with longer and more intense heatwaves. These local changes create important public interest stories, but many journalists avoid climate data because it seems too technical or difficult to understand.

I faced the same challenge while reporting on climate change in Turkey’s Aegean region. The Copernicus Browser and Sentinel satellite imagery offer one of the world’s largest collections of free climate data, but finding information is only the first step. The real challenge is turning scientific observations into stories that readers can understand and relate to.

One piece of advice from Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) climate scientist Francesca Guglielmo shaped the way I approached this project. Rather than focusing on individual temperature records, she said she encourages journalists to explain how different climate indicators work together and how those changes affect people’s lives.

title: Under Pressure, but Undeterred: How the Investigative Press Corps Perseveres in Argentina
content:
Javier Milei had been Argentina’s president for nearly two years when the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) held a session in which participants warned of the “rapid and pronounced” deterioration of freedom of expression in the country.

During the hearing, journalism and civil society organizations testified to their experiences practicing under a flamboyant president who hit the campaign trail with a chainsaw, and who had positioned himself on the side of right-wing antagonists of the press like US President Donald Trump and his former Brazilian counterpart, President Jair Bolsonaro.

The November 2025 hearing revealed data from the Freedom of Expression Monitoring Project of the Argentine Journalism Forum (FOPEA), which showed attacks on the press surged last year to the highest number since tracking began in 2008. In 2025, the report found, there were 278 attacks on freedom of expression, a 55% increase over 2024 and triple the figure from before Milei took office.

title: Investigating Inside Conflict Zones and Areas Controlled by Armed Groups: Lessons from Africa
content:
For investigative journalists in Africa, getting into an area controlled by armed groups may not be the most dangerous part of an assignment. The real challenge is figuring out how to report safely when armed groups control territory, access is restricted, information is unreliable, and the people who speak to you may face reprisals.

Journalists working in these environments make difficult decisions at every stage of an investigation: when it is safe to travel, whom to trust, how to reach sources, how to verify claims, and when to abandon a reporting plan.

Sometimes, staying away from the most dangerous areas and finding other ways to gather evidence becomes the safest option. According to Reporters Without Borders, more than 50 media professionals have been killed in Somalia since 2010, making it one of Africa’s most dangerous countries for journalists. In Mali, insecurity and political instability have restricted journalists’ access to information, while Ethiopia’s conflicts have raised fears of reprisals against journalists. In northern Nigeria, journalists encounter difficulties reporting on terrorist groups, bandits, and other armed actors involved in killings and abductions.

title: Senior Communications Officer
content:
JX Fund supports exiled media from countries where independent reporting is no longer possible due to repression, persecution, and censorship. It provides financial support through grants and complements this with tailored programs responding to the needs of exiled media. To this end, JX Fund collects and curates knowledge and data on the needs, challenges, and achievements of exiled media, conducts research, and connects and facilitates communication between various international actors. Its support programs are developed dynamically and in response to needs, based on the data and observations collected.

They are looking for a Senior Communications Officer to lead the JX Fund’s external communications across media, public audiences, policymakers, institutional donors and private philanthropists.

title: Program Coordinator, Eastern Europe/Central Asia
content:
The Program Coordinator is responsible for CPJ’s work in the region and leads research, documentation, and advocacy on press freedom violations. CPJ is seeking an individual with extensive experience covering press freedom issues in Russia and Eastern Europe, and an excellent understanding of the main challenges across the wider region. The candidate must be based in the ECA region and will be hired via an Employer of Record.

The Program Coordinator role requires a strong background in media, press freedom policy, and advocacy in the ECA region, excellent research and analysis skills, and the ability to work independently and proactively. The role also involves responding to journalist assistance cases, including support for journalists experiencing trauma or post-traumatic situations.
